title: Act I, Scene IV

teacherSummary.text: On the battlements at midnight, as Claudius carouses below, Hamlet criticizes Danish drinking. The Ghost appears and beckons. Despite his friends' fears, Hamlet follows. Marcellus says something is rotten in Denmark.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore

writingPrompts.label: College Junior

writingPrompts.label: College Senior

Let me not burst in ignorance; but tell
Why thy canonized bones, hearsed in death,
Have burst their cerements; why the sepulchre,
Wherein we saw thee quietly inurn’d,
Hath oped his ponderous and marble jaws,
To cast thee up again.

It beckons you to go away with it,
As if it some impartment did desire
To you alone.

Let me not burst in ignorance; but tell
Why thy canonized bones, hearsed in death,
Have burst their cerements; why the sepulchre,
Wherein we saw thee quietly inurn’d,
Hath oped his ponderous and marble jaws,
To cast thee up again.

The king doth wake to-night and takes his rouse,
Keeps wassail, and the swaggering up-spring reels;
And, as he drains his draughts of Rhenish down,
The kettle-drum and trumpet thus bray out
The triumph of his pledge.
A flourish of trumpets, and ordnance shot off, within.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “The air bites shrewdly; it is very cold” slowly and put it in my own words: Waiting on the battlements, Hamlet says the air bites shrewdly and is very cold. Next, craft. I notice the personified air that "bites," which gives the night a hostile edge. The strongest word is “bites”: it makes the cold feel like an attack, adding to the tension. Then, effect. Why does Hamlet comment on the cold air before the Ghost appears? My answer: The small talk about weather fills the nervous wait; the biting air prepares the audience for something supernatural and threatening to appear.
